utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone on this Pre-Defence Conference. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Just for the record, although we do not do it every day, Mr. Harmon and Mr. Tieger for the Prosecution, and Mr. Stewart and Mr. Josse for the Defence, assisted by members of their staff. An agenda has been sent to the parties, including those items suggested by the parties to be included. Unless there's anything else to be raised before we start with the agenda, I suggest to the parties that we just follow the agenda. But I can imagine, Mr. Stewart, that one of the motions you filed, which seems to be moot, that is, a motion for certification for an appeal against the decision to stay, at least the decision on your motion for a stay, that that might be a reason to withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I had better explain as briefly as I can the position there. Yesterday afternoon, we received the Appeals Chamber decision dismissing our appeal against the dismissal of our 98 bis application made in August and presented by Mr. Josse in Court, on the basis that the Appeals Chamber said that we required a certificate, and therefore the appeal was basically not valid on that ground. We received that yesterday afternoon. Yesterday afternoon, we were, in fact, filing, and did in fact file, two motions, including the one -- or application for certification, including the one that Your Honour mentioned. This morning, we are filing, within the next few minutes, really, as soon as somebody is available in the Registry to take it, we are filing, in the light of the Appeals Chamber's decision, an application for an extension of time to apply for a certificate to appeal against the refusal of the 98 bis application and, consequential upon that, if we get that extension of time, then the application for the certificate as well. If our application for extension of time and the application for a certificate were successful, then we would need to present our appeal; it's either a new appeal or our appeal all over again against the refusal of the 98 bis application. In those circumstances, Your Honour, if we did wish then to raise the question of a stay pending appeal, we would have to do it technically by way of a new application, a new motion, and therefore, yes, the result with that two-minute summary is exactly as Your Honour says, that the particular motion for a stay and the application for certification, that's all gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Procedurally, that's a dead duck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Thank you for that. Then since I did not hear any objection against following the agenda as it has been presented, I'd like to start with the first item, overview of disclosure by the Defence, Rule 65 ter (G) material. We received the 65 ter (G) summaries -- yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to address the honourable judges in the course of this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll be given an opportunity later on. Have you informed counsel about what you'd like to raise, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say, Mr. Krajisnik hasn't strictly informed me, but I've got a pretty good idea. But maybe he'll add something else. Your Honour, perhaps I can simply say that. Mr. Krajisnik -- I'm not preventing Mr. Krajisnik himself from answering that question, Your Honour, but that's the position, from where I stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, have you informed Mr. Stewart about what you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add to what Mr. Stewart has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are invited and instructed always to inform counsel, apart from very exceptional circumstances, to inform counsel on any matter you'd like to raise yourself, because counsel could -- at least we cannot exclude that he could assist you in giving proper advice on the matters you'd like to raise, procedural aspects of matters you would like to raise. So you're invited and instructed always to at least communicate with counsel the matters you would like to raise, again, as I said, apart from very, very exceptional circumstances. The Chamber will always consider whether such exceptional circumstances are there upon the indication on your side what the subject of your submission would be. But we'll give you an opportunity later today. Then we return to the item 1 on the agenda, which is overview of disclosure by the Defence. We've received the 65 ter summaries, the list of witnesses. There's still a lot of work to be done, from what I understand. We also received the number of hours involved, which do not exactly fit into what the Trial Chamber has indicated before as the time available to the Defence. But the Chamber also understands that further selections are needed to come to the final list, and of course the Chamber is aware that by allowing the Defence to file a list which is to some extent a provisional list rather than the final list, that we, of course, would not blame the Defence for this moment on giving a couple of hours more than the Chamber indicated that were available. Nevertheless, the total number of hours is of great concern to the Chamber. But we'll leave that to a later stage. Mr. Harmon, the Prosecution has asked to make some submissions on the quality of the Defence 65 ter summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, counsel. I start, Your Honour, with the text of the Rule, Rule 65 ter (G)(1)(b), which requires that the Defence file, and I quote: "A summary of the facts on which each witness will testify." And I underscore the word "facts." Now, this Rule covers two interests. It covers the interest of the Court to be properly informed of what evidence may be presented to it so it can properly manage the case, and it protects the interest of the Prosecution so the Prosecution can be adequately informed of the facts about which each witness will testify so that the Prosecution can prepare adequately for cross-examination. It is our submission, after a very careful review of the extensive filing made by the Defence, that the Defence submissions fall short -- in terms of being factual submissions, they fall short by virtually every standard. I would like to read two such submissions into the record as exemplars. I would not reveal the names of the witnesses, because I don't know to what extent they will be protected witness. I can in private session, if the Court is interested, identify which witness I'm referring to. Let me read from two --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would it be a simple, practical thing if somebody were to jot on a piece of paper which witnesses Mr. Harmon is referring to? I don't mind crossing the court to receive that piece of paper, and Your Honours as well, and then we'll just be able to look, if Mr. Harmon has got two or three in mind. It seems a practical suggestion rather than going in and out of private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Harmon already writing, so he followed your suggestion, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does the Court wish to see the names as well, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Reading from the first name that appears on that list, the summary that we were provided reads as follows: "This witness was BiH and RS assembly deputy from," and it identifies the location. "He was a local authorised commissioner of the RS government. He will give evidence on the following topics: Population and prisoner exchange in relation to Bijeljina, analysis of the causes and motivation for departure of Serbs from Tuzla and Muslims from Bijeljina, general conditions in Tuzla --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Maybe I just too hurriedly wrote it down. This one doesn't seem to be either of the names that was on that piece of paper. Maybe in my hurry to pass on the piece of paper to the Trial Chamber I got it wrong somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it's on Registry page, filing 12540.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't have that pagination, same old story. Is there a page number from the batch of stuff that ... All right. Your Honour, there were two people with the same surname and I took a chance on that. That's what happened. Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll continue reading, if the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me start again at the relevant passage: "He will give evidence on the following topics: Population and prisoner exchange in relation to Bijeljina; analysis of the causes and motivation for departure of Serbs from Tuzla and Muslims from Bijeljina; general conditions in Tuzla on the eve of the conflict; activities of the Special Panther Unit in; knowledge of the A and B variants; the six strategic goals and the authority of Mr. Krajisnik." Now, that, in our submission, Mr. President and Your Honours, is a topical summary, not a factual summary. The second summary I will read -- Mr. Stewart, I don't know if you have the page numbers, but it is in the 12563 of the filing of the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just said I didn't, so I'm afraid I haven't acquired them in the last minute or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In any event, let me read the summary, if the Court has before it the summary. A summary that we were provided for this witness is: "The witness went with Luka Bogdanovic to see if they could talk with someone from the top in Pale. He wanted to talk to Karadzic, but since he was not there, Mr. Krajisnik was the only one available, who greeted them without actually knowing why they came to see him. They soon realised that Mr. Krajisnik knew nothing of the group, and in order to prove it to them, Mr. Krajisnik made a telephone call." That's the end of the summary. In our submission, this is virtually incomprehensible and does not assist us in any way in determining what this witness's evidence is going to be. Now, Your Honour, if I could, I recall that the submission that the Prosecution made pursuant to its 65 ter summaries was filed on the 2nd of May, 2002, and so the summaries that were available to the Defence were in many cases available years before the witness actually took the stand to testify. As witnesses came to testify before this Tribunal, additional factual summaries were provided to the parties. And I would like to pass out one example of a factual summary that we provided to the Court and to counsel. It is the factual summary that relates to Witness Miroslav Deronjic. And if I could pass that out. And if we could compare the factual summary of Deronjic with the factual summaries that I have read from the Defence submissions, it will be evident there's a stark contrast. Now, for your information, Your Honour, this summary was filed with the Court and provided to the Defence on the 14th of January, 2004, and Mr. Deronjic testified on -- about a month later, the 12th to the 19th of February, 2004. So I'll give Your Honours a moment to cast your eye on the factual summary that was provided in the case of this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even without rereading it as a whole, the Chamber has a sufficient impression and sufficient recollection on the type of summary you provided at that time. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, to the extent that any of the Prosecution summaries and the 65 ter submissions that we made to the Court fell short of the mark, it must be remembered that the Defence had available to it copies of witness statements taken by the OTP, copies -- in some cases copies of statements of the same witness taken by the Bosnian authorities, in some cases they had previous testimonies of the witness. In the case that we're confronted with today, with these submissions that have been made by the Defence, we have no statements of these witnesses. We can't fall back on trying to fill gaps in these summaries that have been provided to us through looking at witness statements or previous testimonies or the like. So that's a significant difference as well. I would also submit to Your Honours that as was our practice when witnesses who had been identified by us and whose summaries and statements the Defence had would come to us and see us before they testified, if there were additional facts that were exposed in the course of the conversation we had with the witnesses, we filed written summaries of those facts as soon as was possible. So if you compare what is available to the Prosecution through the 65 ter summaries that the Defence have filed, which are not factual, they are virtually, in large measure, fact-free. And what the Defence had to its advantage, you will see there's a huge disparity between what has been available and what is available to the parties. And in fact, the bottom line is the Defence knew the facts about which each witness would testify. Now, there's jurisprudence in this institution that relates specifically to this subject. I, Your Honour, have been involved in previous litigation in the Krstic case. For example, I was confronted with the same issue, and I raised the same objection. And in that Krstic case, Your Honour, the Court agreed with the objections that I had made and required the Defence to re-file 65 ter summaries. And in fact, they re-filed them on two occasions, because after they re-filed them on the first occasion, there were still deficiencies and the Court required, and the Defence did in fact file, a second filing. I can give Your Honours the dates of those filings and I can give Your Honours the dates of the transcript from the Court discussion, if you wish. Secondly, there is a written decision - let me pass it out, Your Honour - in the Kupreskic case that deals precisely with the issue that we're confronted with today. It's a short decision, Your Honour, and I'll let Your Honours cast your eye on it, and counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a decision that squarely is on point with the issue that we're confronting today. In the Kupreskic case, the Prosecution complained about the summaries that had been submitted by the Defence. And the Court found that the summaries were insufficient factually. They ordered the Defence to provide summaries to the Office of the Prosecutor within two weeks and ordered that if there was a failure to do so, the Prosecution would have the opportunity and be permitted to interview the witnesses whose summaries were deficient. The Court concluded that the failure to provide sufficient summaries impinged on the principle of equality of arms. We believe, Your Honour, and we assert vigorously, that we're entitled to factual summaries, and we insist that they be provided to us. We don't believe it's proper that Mr. Krajisnik should benefit from a wilful non-compliance with the obligations that are imposed upon him by the Rules. And therefore, Your Honour, we would make the following submissions to the Court: One, that the submissions that had been made pursuant to Rule 65 ter (G) by the Defence are not in compliance with the Rule. We would request that the Defence be ordered to resubmit factual summaries to the Prosecution two weeks in advance of the testimony of each witness before he takes the stand to testify; And three, we would request that in the absence of a proper factual summary being provided to the Prosecution about the substance of the witness's evidence, that the Prosecutor be permitted to interview the witness, as was the case in the Kupreskic decision. Those are our submissions, Your Honour, on the factual submissions -- on the submissions under Rule 65 ter. I have other submissions, but I'll defer those, because they relate to exhibits have not yet been submitted as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I understood you well, you take a different course from the course that was taken in the Kupreskic case. Whereas in that case, the Court ordered submission of new summaries two weeks after the list had been provided and what you're actually asking now is that you at least be provided with an adequate summary two weeks before the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking -- what I'm asking is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I would prefer is to have the summaries of all -- factual summaries of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, preferably yesterday and not today. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I would prefer to have them as soon as possible, but at a minimum, two weeks before each witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I've fully understood you. Perhaps the best way of proceeding is that I give an opportunity now, not to go through the whole of the agenda, and give an opportunity to the Defence, unless the Defence would prefer to take a bit more time to reflect on how to respond to the observations made. But if you'd like to respond now, we could hear your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes. Because I respond now, I don't wish it to be thought that the Defence doesn't reflect on things. We do. We just sometimes try and reflect quickly. It does seem more efficient to deal with the matter item by item and give an immediate response. Your Honour, when we saw quality of Defence 65 ter summaries had been placed on the agenda by the Prosecutor, we thought, how sweet. Somebody has finally recognised the effort and all the work done by the Defence. But this is pointedly not so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the problem with summaries. If you say the quality, you never know it will be praising the quality or saying something negative about the quality. I think that's more or less what also is the subject matter that, if you say the witness will testify about the events, then you've got no idea how the witness perceives those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Recovering from my disappointment, Your Honour, that that wasn't the purpose of that item on the agenda and dealing with the substance, I am in fact going to register a mildish, by my standards, mildish protest that it would have been helpful if a simple list of the items that the Prosecution were intending to refer to under this agenda had been communicated. Even if had been communicated to me at the crack of dawn this morning, we could have handled it more satisfactorily and the decision as well that's been referred to. But it doesn't matter. We're used to coping with things at very short notice. The selection of Deronjic as a summary is frankly ludicrous. Everybody knows the position of Deronjic. And the Prosecution's summaries contain some excellent summaries among the hundreds they produced, and dare I even suggest that somewhere among the summaries we've produced under enormous pressure there are some of more than adequate standard even by the -- what the Prosecution require. Your Honour, I'm not going to pretend and submit that the batch of summaries produced by the Defence in these circumstances is up to the standard that the Defence would have wished to produce overall in compliance with the Rules, because they're not, and we made it 100 per cent clear that that would not and could not happen, and it hasn't happened. However, at the risk of just pots calling kettles black and entering into a sort of playground squabble, we would like to just observe that, for example, and this is Witness L, Brcko, on page 3, and my apologies for not notifying in advance, but I didn't know what was happening this morning on this item. We get: "The witness was transferred to Luka and can comment on certain events there. Specifically, the witness will corroborate the testimony of other witnesses in relation to the detention of women at Luka. The witness will also provide testimony about Batkovic camp and the conditions therein." Well, thank you very much. And then another one, not quite sure who this is. He will also testify about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Mr. Stewart, the Chamber is fully aware that Mr. Harmon has sought -- well, let's say what he considered to be the worst examples on your -- in your summaries and certainly has not chosen to present one of his weaker summaries to the Chamber for a comparison. Therefore, the Chamber is certainly aware that there are stronger and that there are weaker summaries and that going through them, that we would find that, if not it all, some portions of Prosecution summaries would not, as you demonstrated already now, would not meet the requirements of the Rule either. I'm more interested in, and the Chamber is more interested, in the suggestion made by Mr. Harmon. Let's not forget the Kupreskic case, the Prosecution was invited to tell exactly where the major shortcomings were and the Chamber is very much interested to know that whether the matter could be resolved in one way or the other. I noticed already that Mr. Harmon has not, like was done in the Kupreskic case, has not asked for a full new filing within two weeks from now, but takes the course that at least two weeks prior to the testimony of the witness, that these summaries are presented in such a way that the Prosecution is better able to prepare for the cross-examination. The Chamber is mainly interested not in how the parties experience the problems, but rather in how they think they could contribute to resolving them. So I therefore would like to invite you to mainly respond to that. And I would say it goes without saying that your position, as far as the time you had available for preparing them, whether you are satisfied with -- that's all sufficiently clear at this moment. We also -- the examples given by Mr. Harmon, of course, are also considered by the Chamber, and these were certainly not examples that would tend to diminish the problem, but it's more like a - how do you call it? - a reading glass or it's enlarged in the presentation. The Chamber is fully aware of that. Could you please then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour. Just 20 seconds to say I didn't suggest Mr. Harmon had picked out the worst examples. I don't know how he made his selection. I'm sure we have even worse in our batch. I wouldn't wish to rise to that challenge. May I say the examples I just gave were picked up by me at random over the last ten minutes from hundreds of pages. So the two passages I read, those are really pretty much at random. I picked a couple of pages and I just looked for paragraphs on those pages. That's what I did. So but moving on from that, Your Honour, we know what the purpose of these 65 ter summaries is, and we'd also say in relation to their decision in Kupreskic, it doesn't tell us anything unless we looked at the 65 ter summaries. It's almost a meaningless decision for these purposes unless we see what the Court is talking about. We know the principles. Your Honour, the Defence would positively wish, provided that there are enough hours in a day and hours in the week and hours in people's lives to do it, we would positively wish to improve the 65 ter summaries. It doesn't do us any good to withhold anything. It doesn't help us for them to be inadequate. It's just a question of timing. We would like to do that as soon as possible, but we've got to fit it in with everything else. But, Your Honour, in principle, the suggestion that two weeks before, we should provide an improved 65 ter summary where necessary is acceptable to the Defence. We will -- well, there's always slippage somewhere, and the Prosecution know that, we know that with some of the Prosecution's stuff. The parties haven't been unreasonable to each other on the occasional slippage. But in principle we accept that. We'd also comment that the opportunity for the Prosecution to interview witnesses, it strikes us as a bit strange perhaps because that opportunity is there anyway. They're entitled to interview anyone they want to will speak to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether there's any property in a witness seems not to be considered in a similar in the different common law traditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't suggest that they're not free to do that anyway. It's just that there are again issues of time for all concerned. If we want to -- if the Prosecution, you know, want to go off in a bus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So no objection in that respect either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's all. So, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both the two weeks and the other matter of interviewing witnesses is now on the record. The position is clear, Mr. Harmon, I take it, that the Chamber will consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we understand, Your Honour, that the essential purpose -- of course, the essential purpose is fairly to enable the other party to prepare for cross-examination. So if on occasions, and Your Honour and the Prosecution I hope will understand, on occasions when there are real problems about communicating sufficiently thoroughly with a witness before he or she actually comes to The Hague, then it may be that on occasions, the 65 ter summary, even the new improved version two weeks ahead, might not be adequate, but we understand that then the earlier we give the Prosecution as much fair information as we can to enable them to prepare for cross-examination, the better, and we accept that obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to make one observation on the matter of the presentations. Even without talking to a witness, if in a summary someone writes down that Mr. Krajisnik knew nothing of the group, you can't make such a summary unless you have a certain group in mind. I mean, the group, if you do not know what the group is, it makes no sense at all. So therefore, I don't know who drafted this summary, but at least being a bit more explicit by identifying the group, Mr. Krajisnik didn't know anything about, or a group perhaps the witness belonged to or the one who accompanied him when they sought to see someone from the top. I think -- at least, I have difficulties in understanding that that group was not known to the one --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I say straight away, we accept that observation unreservedly, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would not have taken one minute more to replace the group by group so-and-so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's what it wouldn't have taken. That's the point. It doesn't take one minute more. It's actually, given the process by which this is done, which I needn't describe, it can sometimes take considerably more than one minute. But -- so that's why it wasn't done at this stage, Your Honour. But apart from the two-week matter we've just discussed, in very broad terms, the Defence accepts the obligation to improve and have a run-through, which is in everyone's interest, and that sort of matter, Your Honour, I would have loved to have those types of matters tidied up and sorted out themselves. But I assure Your Honour the process of tidying up all those points throughout the numerous summaries was one we just did not have time to do. It required a chain of communication and so on. Sometimes an apparently easy point like that is not so easy if the person preparing the summary or preparing this information at the very first stage didn't appreciate the importance of identifying that item, to track back then was very time-consuming. Your Honour, in the Defence's submission here it seems that we don't really have any significant gap between what the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution would wish and what the Defence understand as the fair response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your observations. Mr. Harmon, is there anything more to be said about this subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Only one brief mention, and that is that we have a witness who has been identified, who will be testifying next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And his summary appears for Your Honour's benefit on page 12530. It suffers from the same deficiencies and we would request the Defence immediately pay attention to a proper summary for this witness so we can begin our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are doing and will do in relation to that witness whatever we can to get as much information as we can and to pass on to the Prosecution, as soon as we can, fairly, as much information as they're reasonably entitled to in order to prepare for the witness. We undertake to do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We all understand that we are at a start now, and even if things are less than perfect, Mr. Harmon, I do understand that the Defence is doing its utmost best to provide the information as soon as possible. Next item, 1(b), 92 bis material. Mr. Stewart, we've seen that on the list there appear a number of 92 bis witnesses. I think there were some 23 or something like that. We have not seen yet any decision by the Registrar to appoint a Presiding Officer to meet formalities under Rule 92 bis. That's one issue, a very technical issue. Of course, the Chamber is concerned that the 92 bis statements would not be available in the form needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour wishes me to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I just say that's noted. We're aware of the need to go through the necessary technicalities and formalities and again, we will do our utmost to comply with those. We will also, of course, we'll be keeping our list under review to confirm which of the witnesses we do propose to approach under 92 bis, and of course, in some cases, if, on further consideration, we take the view that they're not necessary at all, then those witnesses will drop out. But, Your Honour, yes, may I just that the point is noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just noticed that of course some formalities which need the involvement of the Registry in 92 bis cases, well, might take some time. I don't know where these witnesses are all located. So there might be some -- if you start early with asking for the appointment of presiding officers, then the chance that you finally will have the statements in time here, that the Prosecution is in a position to express itself on whether it would like to call the witnesses for cross-examination, could be speeded up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed. We need to find either a person authorised or a Presiding Officer appointed by the Registrar in accordance with the Rules and so on. Your Honour, it's priorities, priorities, priorities. For example, this week, we have given priority to making sure, as sure as we can, that this witness arrives next week, et cetera, et cetera, that we're in contact with the Victims and Witnesses Unit. There's only so much that our case manager can do. There's only so much we can do. We believe we are choosing the right priorities at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just so your attention was drawn to it. The Chamber also noticed, and perhaps I should invite Mr. Harmon to comment on that, that the line between acts and conduct of the accused under 92 bis might be a bit problematic. For example, if a witness would say, "I never met Mr. Krajisnik," is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I short-circuit this. We recognise that line. We note the comment. We will consider it. We are aware of the principle. Again, that's something that we will review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And even I can imagine that the parties will exchange their views on that. Because I can imagine that if someone says I never met Mr. Krajisnik, of course that's acts and conduct of Mr. Krajisnik never coming to that witness or the witness never coming to him. At the same time, it might not be something that should be excluded under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We might have an outbreak of common sense, Your Honour. You never know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if there's any development in that respect, the Chamber would like to hear from the parties. Expert witnesses. Mr. Stewart is the next on the list. I don't have to tell you the procedure under Rule 92 bis, that is, presentation of the report, opportunity for the other party to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You don't, Your Honour. We read the Rule. We're well aware of it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would also imply that an appointment on experts -- and again I'm not going into your prior to list, but certainly should not be at the bottom of that list. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have one question, and that is: Under Rule 94 bis, there is a time-limit, and there's sub-part A, where the party has to disclose within the time-limit prescribed by the Trial Chamber, the Pre-Trial Judge. I'm not aware of any time-limit being set, but for our purposes, we would request that such a time-limit be set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In order to give any time-limit for disclosure, of course, the Chamber would not do that blindly. That means that it would invite the Defence to indicate when it expects to receive these reports so that they can be disclosed. One of the advantages of experts that they do a lot of work on their own. Mr. Stewart, could you now or in the near future give us any indication when you expect to receive expert reports you would like to present?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First find your expert is one of our priorities. Your Honour, in the near future, as near as we can, but it will be completely unrealistic for me to offer anything even remotely claiming to be concrete today. But so I may say, Your Honour, as part of 94, we do note it. We do recognise that all concerned need a fair opportunity to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There comes a time, Mr. Stewart, that you've found your experts and that you have requested him to present an expert report, and usually you also discuss with this expert when it will be presented. As soon as the Defence knows from any of the experts they found when they expect to receive the reports, the Chamber would like to be informed so that the time can be set.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour will be informed, certainly, and exactly as you have just requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber would very much like to receive information on when you expect to receive your expert reports within four weeks from now. So that's not to have the expert reports ready, but -- so we expect you to have made arrangements with experts you selected within four weeks from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the first bit, we very much like to receive information on -- we will give the Trial Chamber, of course, that information. And the expectation is noted, and we will again do our very best to meet that expectation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. This is not an order. I mean, we are dealing perhaps with several experts. But the Chamber also wants to prevent that it gets the information on the 20th of February that you expect to receive the report on the 2nd of May next year. That's the kind of things we'd like to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour, completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the best thing, then, would be to -- if you would not be in a position to do that within four weeks, that you report after these four weeks what kept you off from giving this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will certainly give the information, very much like to receive information on when we expect to receive our expert reports. We will certainly give Your Honours that information within four weeks as you request and then we will do our best to meet the expectation in the second limb of what Your Honour said at lines 22 to 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. Then I think we dealt with item 1 on the agenda. Anything else on this item? Item 2. In item 2, under A, it is stated -- well, the Rule is reflected, which says that: "The Trial Chamber shall set the number of witnesses the Defence may call." Under B, that: "The Trial Chamber may call upon the Defence to shorten the estimated length of the examination-in-chief." And then third item, that: "The Chamber shall determine the time available to the Defence for presenting evidence." They're all related. This Chamber is not very much inclined to limit on numbers of witnesses and is more inclined to leave it to the Defence to present the number of witnesses they would like to present in the time allotted for the presentation of the Defence case. That is one. Secondly, until now, nothing has changed in the previous orders by this Chamber, scheduling orders. Nothing has changed up until now on what has been said during the 65 ter meeting on the time available for the presentation of the Defence case, and nothing has changed yet in the more recent scheduling orders which say that the time-limit is as was set before. At the same time, the Chamber is confronted now, if I do understand -- if my recollection is right, with case presentation, in chief only, of 1.007 hours, I think the last was. It doesn't need a lot of words to tell the parties that that is not coming close to anything acceptable. On the other hand, it perhaps doesn't make that much sense to start a large debate on that list, where we all know that it's still a provisional list. The Chamber, therefore, is inclined at this moment to follow its previous scheduling orders. At the same time, the Chamber is aware that when the Defence case is presented and when there has been a revised list of witnesses, perhaps including different numbers of hours needed for examination-in-chief, that the proof of the pudding is in the eating. Finally, what the Chamber wants, the Chamber wants to give the Defence a fair opportunity to present its case. That is most important. That is what makes a trial fair. At the same time, the Chamber wants to avoid that by an inefficient use of Court time, more time is taken than is necessary. Therefore, even if the Chamber would at this moment restrict itself to the previous orders given, scheduling orders, that does not mean that if a witness for this reason has been, let's say, reduced from four hours to two hours, and if during these two hours, relevant matters are presented in an efficient way, and if there would be one relevant matter not being dealt with, that the Chamber would not allow another 20 minutes or half an hour to complete such an efficient examination of a witness. That's the general approach of the Chamber. But before giving any final decisions, to the extent possible at all at this moment, given the provisional character of the witness list and given the uncertainties in respect of certain witnesses - not all of them may be found that easily - the Chamber would like to hear any further submissions, but then not, in view of the 1.000 hours presented for examination-in-chief, but on a realistic basis, from the parties. Perhaps Mr. Stewart, you're the first one to take the floor and add whatever you'd like to, or to submit whatever you'd like to submit in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in the first place, Your Honour, I'd just like to offer an important clarification. The 1.000 hours, 999 hours, it doesn't make any difference. The 1.000 hours is not - and we had hoped to make that clear - is not what the Defence are submitting are suggesting is necessary for the presentation of the Defence case. That 1.000 hours is simply the arithmetical aggregate of the estimates in the list of witnesses as it stands. The other figure given at the end of our list, which is the more important figure, is 800 hours, and that 800 hours is not like with like, because that 800 hours is the gross figure, including, in line with the guidelines that were imposed during the Prosecution case on Defence cross-examination, including a 60 per cent allowance, based on those estimates for individual -- well, no, in fact not based on those individual estimates. 60 per cent allowance for cross-examination and then an allowance based on past experience for Bench questions, re-examination, and so on. So, Your Honour, the figure, depending on what one means in the end by the time available for the Defence for presenting evidence, talking about the in chief evidence in the first place, it follows that the figure put forward by the Defence at the moment is far, far lower than the 1.000 hours. And Your Honour, that figure is, in broad terms -- one could do the detailed arithmetic, but in broad terms, it is asking for the same time as the Prosecution for presentation of evidence in chief, but with the important consideration that more is added on to reflect the fact that Mr. Krajisnik himself, not uniquely, but certainly not a standard practice in this Tribunal, Mr. Krajisnik himself will be giving evidence. So, Your Honour, that's a mission that can be developed. But what I do suggest, Your Honour, is that with a certain amount of -- with that clarification from the Defence, and with this observation, Your Honour, that of course Rule 73 ter does make it clear, and we rather understand that as being implicit in what Your Honour has just said, it does make it clear that whatever provisional decisions have been made in the past, the question of time for presentation of the Defence case can and must only be in the end worked out, considered, and ordered by the Trial Chamber in the light of full consideration of the material which has been filed under 65 ter, in accordance with the provisions of 73 ter. So that's where we are. But, Your Honour, it may be -- the Defence suggests that with those preliminary observations and that clarification of the Defence position, it might in fact be helpful then briefly to know what the Prosecution position is in relation to what I've just said, supplementing what Your Honours and the Prosecution already have on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's unclear to me exactly how many hours the Defence estimates in its case. I calculated that it would take 46 and a half weeks, five-day trial sessions, if we followed the number of hours that were indicated in the Defence submission. I know that's clearly not going to be the case. But ultimately, Your Honours restricted the amount of hours the Prosecution could present its case in chief. It was 450 hours. I referred to the draft procedural guidelines that were issued by this Trial Chamber. And we came in -- I don't have the figures at my fingertips, but at around 275 or 285 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would add the examination-in-chief and re-examination, you would come to approximately 290 hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the proposition that we saw when we received the submissions by the Defence of approximately 1.000 hours seemed to us to be unrealistic. I am quite confident the Defence intends to continue to work on that estimate, and at this point I think that it is something that bears no additional comments until we see a more realistic estimate of time by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder sometimes if anybody listens when I speak. I've had that experience in my personal life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You made clear that the thousand hours were not your -- perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's just not helpful if the Prosecution just ignore what I've just said and treat it as if it's what I've just expressly stated it isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But wouldn't be it a good idea that you then try, in two minutes, what exactly you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, all over again, Your Honour, what I just explained?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You came to the 800 hours and, in relation to the time given to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I see the point, Your Honour. Yes, it was 280 hours. We have the actual figures off the Court's computer. The Prosecution took 280 hours for examination-in-chief and 9.7 hours for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the 290 hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's exactly where Your Honours -- for Mr. Harmon's information, that's where Your Honour's figure of 290 hours comes from. Your Honour, the one should, and this requires careful consideration and review as well, one should bear in mind that a significant number of witnesses - I think it's in the 90s - but a significant number of witnesses gave evidence under 92 bis, and not only that, but a significant number of witnesses, not in that sort of range of 90s, but important witnesses as well, particularly in the last two or three months of the Prosecution case, were dealt with by robust application of the 89(F) procedure. So that the time taken, as shown on the face of the computer printouts of 280 hours for examination-in-chief, in fact hides the bare figures, hide really in substance a considerable addition in the real presentation of the Prosecution case. So that if one -- and that's not an easy, off-the-cuff calculation to do, and in the end it's not a calculation. There has to be judgement and assessment there. But it's pretty significant. And Your Honours will have a good idea of how much is involved there. We could probably -- again, this requires time. Certainly not something to which we could possibly have given the time over the last week. But one could sit down for a few hours and one could go through the list of 92 -- maybe that's a good idea, Your Honour, to go through the list of 92 bis witnesses and have a look at how 89(F) was used, and come to what in substance would be a real figure for the Prosecution presentation of evidence in chief. But just off the cuff, and the 73 ter orders, we submit, ought not to be done off the cuff, actually, that this does require, all concerned, to give more consideration to it, which will fit in with the fact that there will be some changes in the witness list and so on. But just off the cuff, it's likely that in substance, if we're comparing like with like, or attempting to do that, the Prosecution evidence in chief runs out at something like 350 hours, that 70 hours have got sort of saved by the very widespread use of 92 bis and the robust use of 89(F) at the end. We submit that it's something of that order. Now, of course, as we proceed with the Defence case, it may be that corresponding savings can be made. But, Your Honour, the Defence, and Mr. Krajisnik, must at least, and are entitled to reserve the prima facie position that it may be very important for Your Honours to hear the witnesses. And it was to some extent, although there was, realistically, fairly heavy pressure brought on timing by the Trial Chamber, but in many instances, the Prosecution voluntarily and very cooperatively adopted and endorsed the 89(F) procedure. We're not going to be on the Defence side and we hope we never are unnecessarily obstructed. We reserve the right to be necessarily obstructed, Your Honour, doing our job properly for Mr. Krajisnik. But, Your Honour, the Prosecution case, where we're starting from here is that if the Prosecution case was in substance 350 hours in chief, we can perhaps treat re-examination as, if you like, de minimis or it can come in somewhere else in the equation here. What we do is we take 350, we add on 60 per cent of 350, which I think is 210. That gives 560. We perhaps then do add on some few hours for re-examination, perhaps add on -- let's just add on ten, then. You get 570. So we get to 570 straight off on that calculation. And that's not at all unrealistic. And then we add, for serious consideration, the fact that Mr. Krajisnik is entitled to present witnesses that are not him speaking in his own defence, but other people giving evidence that we call on his behalf. But he himself then gives very substantial -- it's obviously got to be very substantial evidence in his defence and is then cross-examined. And one aspect that will obviously not have escaped Your Honour's notice is that the estimate, and as Your Honour's comments just now recognised, an estimate is not a maximum. It is an estimate. So it may have to be gone over with certain witnesses. It may be that we will get in well under the estimate with some witnesses. But the estimate for Mr. Krajisnik is obviously not an easy estimate to make at this stage. But Your Honours can see from the 65 ter summary, which was not selected for criticism by the Prosecution this morning, 65 ter summary in relation to Mr. Krajisnik, that it's a very large number of topics and looking at any one of those topics, almost any one of those topics, that topic on its own is going to take a considerable time to deal with properly. So that the estimate of evidence for Mr. Krajisnik is rightly very substantial. We do expect, but it's up to them in the end, we do expect that the Prosecution would be likely to want their 60 per cent -- or to use the 60 per cent guideline allocation in relation to Mr. Krajisnik, but that's up to them, of course, when the time comes. But on that footing, and on the basis of that arithmetic, that's how we get to -- not the thousand. The thousand is just arithmetic. It's nothing to do with accepting obviously the -- there's a link between the witnesses and that figure ultimately. But it's not the thousand hours. That 800 hours, which is a gross figure, is the figure one should work from. And it is on this basis that so far, and we face this head on, this Trial Chamber has, well, say talked, but given clear indications for a very long time that it contemplates that the Defence should be allowed, I think it's 60 per cent or perhaps it's -- perhaps it was 66. I think it's been 60 per cent of the Prosecution time for presentation of its case for presentation of the Defence case. Your Honour, that is something which the Defence does not, with respect, endorse. In the Milosevic case and in the Oric case, equality of arms was regarded by the Trial Chamber as entitling the Defence to have the same time as the Prosecution. And Your Honour, the simple yardstick -- comments have been made, but there's been no all-round consideration of it. There have been no submissions on it. There's been no hearing dealing with that particular issue. This is the time to do it. All these matters, in principle, had to await this stage of the proceedings, had to await the 73 ter application with the material which the Court is directed to consider for the purposes of decisions under 73 ter. This is where we're at, to consider now what is the correct allocation. Of course, 73 ter does contemplate there are to be some directions by the Court that set limits. That's obvious. We don't suggest that. They're all subject, of course, to judicial consideration in the circumstances in future as to whether any changes or adjustments are justified. But, Your Honour, that's the explanation, and we hope that that's helpful not just to Your Honours but also to the Prosecution, in understanding what it is then that we are saying. So perhaps, Your Honour, with that clarification, perhaps the Prosecution would like to reconsider observations in relation to this aspect of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in trying to come to a calculation of what the Defence will take is obviously quite difficult for the Prosecution to enter into that debate. Ultimately, the Court has to make a decision on what it deems to be a reasonable balance between a fair trial and the proper and efficient running of this case. I note, for example, when I went through the 65 ter summaries, that the Defence intended to elicit evidence about 17 municipalities that aren't even in the indictment. And there are multiple witnesses for municipalities that are not listed in the indictment. It seems to me that that's a proper area that the Trial Chamber can consider when it assesses the information that's before it and the amount of hours that are suggested will be required. Because it seems to me, in looking at these summaries, that evidence on those municipalities will rarely be relevant to what has been presented in respect of the Prosecution's case and the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the observation just made by Mr. Harmon remain not unnoticed, the fact that quite a number of witnesses are on your list which would give testimony on municipalities that are not part of the indictment. I'm not saying that for that reason it could not be relevant, but it certainly raises the question of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it raises head on this observation straight away, which is that Mr. Harmon's observation and the implications of Mr. Harmon's observation are fundamentally flawed. The Prosecution allege a former Yugoslavia-wide, and then at the very least, in relation to this defendant, a Bosnia and Herzegovina-wide joint criminal enterprise. Their case rests on coordinated activities. That's the way they present it, the actions of the JNA, the actions of the VRS, and so on. The Prosecution selects the municipalities on which they wish to concentrate, sometimes for the purpose of what are called other aspects. It's all the case against Mr. Krajisnik. Some municipalities chosen primarily for detention camps, some municipalities chosen primarily for destruction of cultural heritage, some municipalities chosen specifically for population movement, some municipalities chosen for killings. Your Honour, the absolute, essential thrust of the case against Mr. Krajisnik is the joint criminal enterprise, and everything else spreads out from that. That selection, if it turns out to be selectivity, actually demands that the Defence consider whether evidence from other municipalities casts light on that. So, Your Honour, it's not only that such evidence may be relevant, but it is that the whole point in relation to this matter on the Prosecution side is absolutely, fundamentally flawed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is quite clear that a lot of steps still have to be taken until we come to a final determination. And as I said before, although the Chamber is usually firm in not deviating too easily from its earlier decisions, it's not only a matter, as you've emphasised, Mr. Stewart, to review the present situation in light of the submissions made at this moment, but there's also a continuous monitoring of how the presentation of a case develops. Therefore, if a certain number of hours would be set, and if it turns out that this number of hours could be met easily by the Defence, and at the same time, the Defence would not use its time efficiently, that might even cause a reduction of time. The Chamber has interfered in the presentation of the Prosecution's case as well, as far as numbers of witnesses and numbers of 92 bis witnesses are concerned. Similarly, if it turns out that on the basis of the determination of the time allotted to the presentation of the Defence case, that in the most -- even if done in the most efficient way, substantial portions of information would not reach the Chamber. Due to this limitation in time, the Chamber should then change the numbers of hours allotted in order to receive that information. The issue has been raised before. To what extent the 10th of March would be a kind of a final -- it's what the Chamber has decided until now, but the Chamber -- we have thoroughly considered the matter. We'll constantly monitor how the Defence case is presented, relevance, efficiency, et cetera. If there's anything else the parties would like to bring to our attention at this moment, we'd like to hear it. If not, we'll move to the next item on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, we understand from the observations Your Honour has just made that the matter then -- well, before final decisions are made on these important limits and times and numbers under 73 ter, that there is going to be further consideration. The reason I say that, Your Honour, is that the Defence -- certainly quite a lot of ground has been covered and a lot of valuable observations have been made by Your Honour this morning, an opportunity for the Defence, when we get the chance to take it, to consider even just what's been said this morning would really be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just see whether I've fully understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Time to think about it, Your Honour, in about six words, is what I'm asking. That summarises what I've just said in the last dozen lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you say "time to think about it," you're asking -- in order to make further submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when? Do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Later today is what we had in mind, Your Honour, yes. We try to think quickly, Your Honour. We're not talking about days or anything like that, but later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I don't want to be misunderstood. I'm not saying determinations could not be made, but I'm not saying that this Chamber takes a flexible approach. Even it might raise some strong comments. At the same time, the Chamber doesn't want to be rigid once a determination has been made, and when it turns out that it's wrong what we did, we'll change it, in whatever direction. Then we move to the next agenda item. We could not finish it before the next break. But perhaps we could start with the first one, other issues. Mr. Stewart, you introduced the matter, scheduling of Mr. Krajisnik's own personal evidence. I think you referred to that already before. I'll try to find it again. Because I do understand that you had not in mind the testimony to be given by Mr. Krajisnik but the testimony to be heard on the basis of his wishes for witnesses. Is that correct or is it a wrong understanding? Perhaps you'll explain 3(a)(1).

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I did mean the evidence to be given by Mr. Krajisnik himself in the witness-box. That is what I meant, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not encouraging the other category of evidence as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to avoid that there was any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please introduce the matter you'd like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was really just that: That the Defence would have preferred, and I think I made this clear at the 65 ter Conference in August, the Defence would always have preferred Mr. Krajisnik to be the first witness in the conventional manner, and the conventional manner has underneath it all sorts of real, practical purposes. It's both from the point of view of the Trial Chamber and the point of view of the Defence, the interests generally coincide that one should, if at all possible, put the defendant up as the first witness, and that would be our preferred course. However, Your Honour, it is simply not, and that's what we indicated at the 65 ter Conference, it is simply not practically possible. And I just really wanted to put on record that that remains the position. And also, that, although again we're talking about a piece of string which is long, but we don't know how long, that being in that position and preparing for that evidence -- and if I say preparing Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour won't misunderstand us to be suggesting anything improper there. In the broadest sense, preparation of Mr. Krajisnik and preparation of Mr. Krajisnik's evidence is going to take a long time and we are going to have to do it alongside everything else we're going to have to do. Your Honour, may I presume to just move up item 3(a)(b)? Would Your Honour allow me to move 3(a)(b) up the agenda at this point and make a comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That seems a very practical matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is a practical matter. It is an important practical matter. When we sit in the mornings - we have on occasion made this request before - when we sit in the mornings, we are in practice unable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a matter of visiting Mr. Krajisnik. We know the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Everybody's tired. We don't get time. Your Honour, it really is essential that we regularly are able to have access to Mr. Krajisnik and he to us, in the mornings. So that the request -- Your Honours have a preference for mornings. As a matter of fact, I personally have a preference for the mornings. It's not always shared by all my Defence team every day, but it's not a democracy, the Defence team, Your Honour. But what we do request as a compromise is: Would Your Honours consider alternating morning and afternoon weeks? That ought not to be too unpleasant or disruptive for anybody, and it would go a very long way to helping deal with this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is mainly a matter of agreeing with the Trial Chamber that uses the same courtroom. Usually it's no major problem to claim afternoon sessions. It's rather the other way around, if you want more morning sessions, you might have a problem. And, of course, for Fridays, it's even very much welcomed if you take the afternoon session. I'll discuss the matter with my colleagues, and what I can tell you is that in the previous case over which I presided I was fully able to reach an agreement with the other Trial Chamber to alternate morning and afternoon sessions week by week. So I'm quite confident. I do understand that you considered this already a bit to be a compromise. You might even prefer to always sit in the afternoons, which would grant you more time in the morning, and I fully understand what the advantages are, although your personal preference, of course, would be morning sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My absolute personal preference. That's purely personal, is to get up in the morning and get on with it, Your Honour. But that's not really -- that's not the issue. It's -- yes, we are very grateful for that, Your Honour, and we welcome cooperation on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we should not focus primarily on our personal preferences, but rather focus on the opportunity for the Defence to, as efficiently as possible, prepare the presentation of its case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, are we at the point of a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately, yes, because we started at 9.37, and so we spent now one and a half hours. If there's anything brief to be discussed at this moment, we could do it, but no more than five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's just that I have no more to say on those two items that we put together, 3(a)(1) and 3(a)(4). I'm sorry, there is the Prosecution, of course. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. I'll give an opportunity to the Prosecution. But first a question. You say scheduling of Mr. Krajisnik's own personal evidence and then you tell us that very much in the -- I would say in the English tradition, very much at this moment a bit against the American case-law, from what I understand, that you'd prefer to have the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik first, that you're still aiming at -- do you have any idea at this moment? I mean, I take it that you're scheduling your own activities as well -- whether we could expect the evidence of Mr. Krajisnik at the middle of the case, just before the middle of the case, at second half of the case, but then perhaps preferably before expert testimony? Could you give us any indication?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I beg Your Honour's pardon. I should have added something which I certainly -- in my mind, I should have added something. Your Honour, our present intention would be to make Mr. Krajisnik the first witness on the first day that the Court sits after the Christmas/New Year break. That has, of course, the very important implication that we then do not run the risk of Mr. Krajisnik being, as it were, stranded in the witness-box over that recess, with all the problems about communication. So that would be our present intention, that we suggest, Your Honour, that in the circumstances, if we can't put him up straight away, that that's the sensible approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would mean that if you would stick to your 175 hours -- yes, it was 175 hours, where we usually have 20 effective hours a week in Court, that would mean that that would take approximately nine weeks on from early January, which would bring us somewhere at the end of March or mid-March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we are well aware that that is the, if you like, the arithmetical and chronological consequence, Your Honour, which -- of course, it ties in not with the Trial Chamber's hopes and expectations and indications in the past; is does tie in with what we're submitting. But, Your Honour, I'm not at this stage -- I hope Your Honours wouldn't expect me to -- I'm not in any way resiling from the 175-hour estimate, though I do undertake to give it detailed, careful consideration item by item and overall as a matter of reasonable priority. It's a difficult one, that, Your Honour, and of course I will do that. And I don't want Mr. Krajisnik to have to be in that box for weeks and weeks longer than he absolutely needs to be, Your Honour. And it may very well be, and in principle it should be, that if we take that time, if proper time is available to us to prepare Mr. Krajisnik to give evidence, according to what I've indicated, well, at least that's going to be more efficient than putting him up sooner when we haven't had a chance to do the job at all thoroughly. What that means in terms of the estimate, I don't know. But Your Honour is, well, is absolutely right. We face that. That is the arithmetical and chronological consequence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even without knowing when you would intend to call Mr. Krajisnik as a witness, of course the Chamber has already considered the number of 175 hours. And it might not surprise you that considering this estimate, the Chamber became again aware of the importance of monitoring on how the presentation of evidence develops. Especially if we're talking about nine weeks, then the Chamber would certainly keep a close eye on efficiency, relevance, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's entirely proper, Your Honour. We could not possibly suggest anything different. And that would be the normal obligation of the Trial Chamber. We would entirely accept that. We have absolutely no wish to be inefficient with the result that Mr. Krajisnik has to spend endless unnecessary days in the witness-box. That's -- we all have the same object there, Your Honour. But there is some link, but perhaps, Your Honour, I won't go into it now, with Your Honour's permission. There is, of course, some link between these issues and 3(a)(8)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, perhaps I might leave that for the moment for its proper place in the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break now. After the break we'll first resume with agenda item 3(a)(2) and (3) and then continue with 5 and following. We adjourn until 20 minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume the pre-Defence conference: We were at agenda items 3(a)(2), efficient use of electronic files. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. We put this on the agenda, first of all, we try to do this, but it was also this, Your Honour: Of course, particularly when the parties are preparing their cases, naturally, they have all sorts of material which they legitimately wish to keep to themselves in the course of preparation. However, there is in this case an enormous amount of material, and is electronic material, which is public, and certainly public on two levels, some of it, in a sense, entirely public, because the hard-copy equivalent is already well in the public domain. And there's in a sense a more limited form of public which is it's certainly available to everybody concerned with this case, Trial Chamber, Prosecution, Registry, so far as they're interested, et cetera, et cetera. And of course it passes through their hands, often. So what we -- as well as a simple efficiency, if you like, on the day-to-day, week-to-week level, which I'll come to in a moment. We have been concerned on the Defence side to make sure that, as far as possible, there isn't duplication of evidence and duplication of work here, so that, for instance, if either the Trial Chamber or the Prosecution, or I've got to say this would be a rather rare case, if the Defence has material collated, of that public nature, in either category, collated in some very convenient, usable form, then in the interests of just generally getting on with this case, that there isn't in principle any reason why that shouldn't be shared if it's not too fantastically inconvenient. We have one current example. I don't know whether Ms. Pitcher, Ms. Kelly Pitcher, who is in Court this morning, has actually sent that -- oh, she hasn't sent the communication yet. I know that because she and I have to discuss it a little bit more. But I will illustrate by reference to this example. Mr. Treanor's evidence, vast quantities of material, we are not struggling, exactly, but we can see that it is a very time-consuming exercise for us to track down all the stuff that Mr. Treanor referred to and considered in a convenient, electronic form, and identify it and make sure it's in the right folders and make sure we can find it easily. It occurs to us. We don't know. We're going to ask the question. But it has occurred to us that either possibly any of the Office of the Prosecutor or the Trial Chamber or Mr. Treanor himself, who can -- and his team, who can then pass it through, may have that material in a readily manageable, structured form, that in principle, there can't be any objection in handing it over to us. That's one illustration, Your Honour, and we raise it because we know that sometimes when we ask the Prosecution to do something, they understandably sometimes say, well, we've got a lot of things to do, we've got shortage of time, we've got shortage of hours, we've got an awful lot of work to do. And then we sometimes get into a sort of discussion, well, is ten hours or is five hours of Prosecution team time a fair trade-off to save the Defence 30 hours of work? We'd suggest it is. But the trouble is, of course, it's a call on the Prosecution's time. So we raise that, Your Honour, but in principle, we're really just asking, if you like, for the Trial Chamber's endorsement for the notion that these requests, well, can and should be made in the interests of saving everybody's work and time and avoiding duplication, and as far as possible, and we realise it's a bit one-sided because we're not able to offer on the Defence side, frankly, any great trade-off of assistance in this area to either the Trial Chamber or the Prosecution. We realise it's a one-sided matter. But we're asking really for endorsement that in principle such requests can and should be made and that they will be as favourably considered as can reasonably be managed. That's number one. Secondly, on the question of just day-to-day management, I'll just say this: It is the Defence's intention to try to use electronic material as much as possible. We will try to produce, when we -- and it may be a little while before we can get such a system up and running. We will try to produce material as much as possible in usable, when we come to exhibits, usable electronic form. We will try to produce, in the way that the Prosecution, with some rather more formal technological resources, try to produce hyperlinks and so on. We will try to do that. Many members of the Defence team at least have the ability, they certainly have that, and in some cases, the technical knowledge, but we'll try to increase the technical knowledge to match the ability. That's that item. That's what it was about, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's an announcement which is of course much applauded by the Chamber that you'll try to make optimal use of electronic techniques in order to assist everyone. The other issue is a question of which I'm afraid that the Chamber might not be of much avail to you, Mr. Stewart, because we usually do not reformat the material we receive. So the accessibility for the Chamber, I take it, is exactly the same as it is now for the Defence. Mr. Harmon, the request is there that if there would be material available in such a format or context, that it would assist the Defence to more easily access that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In principle, Your Honour, we, the Defence and the Prosecution have had a cooperative relationship on that. Where there is a resistance point by the Prosecutor's office, because of limited staff and resources, is to request repeatedly the same materials that have been provided earlier. So, for example, on the Treanor materials, I am informed by Ms. Javier that we provided all of the Treanor materials on a DVD to the Defence. And I don't know, since I haven't heard the exact nature of the request, what it is, but if it is to resubmit the same materials on a DVD, then that's unnecessary. We normally try to direct the Defence to the date and time when we submitted that to them and refer them to that, and that seems to us to be the efficient way to approach the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any issue of disclosure to the former Defence and the present Defence team or is that not an issue in this example which plays any role?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Usually we find a solution, Your Honour. There are examples of times when the matters have been disclosed to the former Defence team, re-disclosed to the present Defence team, re-requested again, you know, and that's where we have the resistance point. But by and large, there is a cooperative relationship and we will accept the requests. We'll consider every request. However, our first reaction will be, if it has been provided earlier in an electronic format, to indicate that's the case and tell them when they got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, that's helpful, and I don't mean to be grudging if I say it's helpful as far as it goes. We -- my Defence team know that my standing instruction to them, and it's often specifically repeated, my standing instruction to them is that they must always look for something first before asking the Prosecution. And that is, they know that. Sometimes they don't like it. But it is a repeated instruction, and they understand that. And of course, there's a judgement about what's a reasonable search, but that's my instruction to them. We obviously, Your Honour, we try to avoid simply asking for exactly what we've had before. It's -- there's no value in having an elaborate debate on this before we have considered in detail, for example, in relation to Mr. Treanor submitted the precise request. But, Your Honour, what I don't expect we will do at all is simply ask for the same stuff that was given to us on a DVD. I don't say it never happens, but we're not in the habit of losing DVDs.
